chapters.summary: Chair Selvena Brooks-Powers introduces herself and welcomes attendees to the hearing on the Department of Probation's organizational strategy. She notes the committee will also hear Intro 1104 on providing youth information about the criminal legal process.
chapters.title: Chair Brooks-Powers convenes hearing on Department of Probation organizational strategy

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Silvina Brooks-Powers, Chair of the Committee on Criminal Justice.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I want to welcome everyone to today's hearing on the organizational strategy of the Department of Probation.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers describes the Department of Probation's responsibilities, including supervision, court investigations, juvenile intake, and connecting clients to services. She says the department's organizational approach affects officer-client interactions, outcomes, and how families navigate court.
chapters.title: Chair outlines DOP responsibilities and impact of organizational approach

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The Department of Probation plays an important role in New York City's criminal legal system.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Its responsibilities extends beyond supervising individuals in the community to include court-related investigations, juvenile intake and adjustment,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and connecting people under supervision with services that support their stability and successful completion of probation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The department's organizational approach affects how these responsibilities are carried out, how officers interact with the people they supervise, what the outcomes are for people under department supervision,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and how effectively young people and families navigate the court system.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says DOP has faced staffing shortages, retention problems, and caseload management challenges. She notes a reported 23% vacancy rate with 255 vacancies, including 210 probation officers, and concerns about eliminated court liaison positions.
chapters.title: Chair cites DOP staffing shortages, 23% vacancy rate, and court liaison concerns

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In recent years, the department has faced significant challenges related to staffing shortages, employee retention, caseload management, and the direction of its supervision policies.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: As of March, the department reported a vacancy rate of approximately 23%, 255 vacancies, 210 of which were probation officers.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The elimination of court liaison officer positions under the previous administration raised concerns about coordination with family court.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and the ability to identify opportunities for adjustment before young people enter formal court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The return of court liaison functions, along with changes to caseload assignments and staff requirement efforts, makes it important to examine how the department

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: is organized today and how these decisions affect the agency's work.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers notes Commissioner Goodwin's appointment in January and says the hearing will examine changes under new leadership. She says the committee will look at staffing, caseloads, court coordination, services, and data-driven decision-making.
chapters.title: Chair frames hearing around new DOP leadership and organizational changes

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The department has been under new leadership since Commissioner Goodwin's appointment in January.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Today's hearing is an opportunity to hear directly from the department about the change that leadership has brought.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What remains in development, and how those changes are impacting probation officers and those under their supervision.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: As we examine the department's organizational strategy, we must consider both the conditions facing probation officers and the experiences of the people under their supervision.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Effective probation requires trained and supported staff, manageable and appropriately structured caseloads, coordination with the courts, and access to services that address the needs contributing to justice system involvement.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Today, the committee will examine the department's current staff and management practices, its approaches to assigning and supervising cases, and the role of the community-based programs in supporting successful outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We will also consider how the department evaluates program effectiveness.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: and uses available data to guide decisions about services and resources.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers introduces Intro 1104, which would require DOP to give youth accused of crimes notices explaining the criminal legal process. The notices would cover adjustment, petitions, pre-sentencing reports, dispositions, defense providers, and protections before intake interviews.
chapters.title: Chair introduces Intro 1104 on youth notices and intake protections

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In addition to today's topic, the committee will be hearing introduction number 1104, sponsored by myself, in relation to providing youth accused of crimes with information about the criminal legal process.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: This bill would require the Department of Probation to provide young people accused of crimes with notices explaining the criminal legal process.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: These notices would provide information on adjusting cases, filing petitions, pre-sentencing reports, and potential dispositions.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The notices would also provide information regarding different criminal defense providers in New York City that the young person may contact.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The bill would also require that before beginning an intake interview with a probation officer, a young person be read the protections afforded them during the interview.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Young people and families should understand how this process works before they begin it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: A notice delivered at first contact would give them the information they need to make informed decisions, and I look forward to working with the department and our stakeholders to get it right.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I would also like to take a moment to thank my staff and committee staff for their hard work.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Jahari Frazier, counsel to the committee.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Owen Brady, my policy and budget director.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And Renee Taylor, my chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I look forward to a productive discussion with the department and our other stakeholders about the direction of probation in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The progress being made to strengthen its operations and the steps needed to ensure that the department carries out its responsibilities

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: effectively while supporting rehabilitation, accountability, and successful outcomes for the people it serves.

chapters.summary: Sharon Goodwin introduces herself as Commissioner of the New York City Department of Probation. She introduces First Deputy Commissioner Robert Eusebio and Deputy Commissioners Wayne McKenzie, Tina Ruggieri, and Stacey Decimore.
chapters.title: Commissioner Goodwin introduces herself and DOP leadership panel

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Brooks-Powers and members of the Criminal Justice Committee.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I am Sharon Goodwin, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Seated with me today is First Deputy Commissioner Robert Eusebio and Deputy Commissioners

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Wayne McKenzie, Tina Ruggieri, and Stacey Decimore, who oversee legal and external affairs, adult operations, and juvenile operations, respectively.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify about the important work of the Department of Probation and its organizational strategy.

chapters.summary: Goodwin says the department's organizational strategy can be summed up as 'what works,' or evidence-based practice. She describes it as a return to core values and helping clients get out and stay out of the justice system.
chapters.title: Goodwin says DOP strategy is 'what works' and evidence-based practice

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: The Department of Probation's organizational strategy can be summed up in just two words, what works.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Referred to in the field as evidence-based practice.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: It is a return to our core values, a return to working with people and the larger community to help the clients get out and stay out of the justice system.

chapters.summary: Goodwin says she started as an intern 40 years ago and has held nearly every position in the probation officer title series. She says restoring the agency to its fundamentals has been her core focus.
chapters.title: Goodwin recounts 40-year probation career and restoring fundamentals

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: My entire career has been with New York City probation.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: 40 years ago, I started as an intern.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Fresh out of Utica College, now Utica University.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: My alma mater, I have held nearly every position in the probation officer title series, including probation officer trainee, probation officer, court liaison officer, supervising

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: probation officer, branch chief, assistant commissioner, deputy commissioner, and now commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Restoring the agency to its fundamentals, to what works, has been my core focus.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Today, I will provide an update on some of the best practices implemented thus far.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Staffing and recruitment, right-sizing caseloads, and rebuilding relationships.

chapters.summary: Goodwin says probation's most important asset is its people and notes the agency had a 23% vacancy rate. She says the vacancy rate has decreased 8% and describes reinstituting the probation officer trainee title to hire college graduates while they gain casework experience.
chapters.title: Goodwin addresses staffing vacancies and reinstated probation officer trainee title

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Without question, probation's most important asset is its people.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We cannot do this work without quality, experienced staff.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: For the past three years, probation had the highest vacancy rate of any city agency, 23%.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Thankfully, we are beginning to see results from our staffing and recruitment focus as our vacancy rate has decreased 8%.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: This has had a marked impact on staff morale and workload, and ultimately the resources and attention available for the people we serve.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Here's how we got there.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Probation officers are one of the most highly educated and credentialed civil service titles in New York City government.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: title series requires a bachelor's degree and two years of casework experience.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: To hire college graduates who do not have yet the casework experience, like I didn't when I first started, we reinstituted the probation officer trainee title.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: This additional civil service title meets the field requirements while on the job, allowing us to hire and train more officers more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: The next probation officer training exam will be open for filing November 5th through the 25th, 2026.

chapters.summary: Goodwin says the probation training academy was optimized from 5.1 months to 3.5 months while meeting state mandates. She says two academies graduated 57 officers this year, with about 50 more expected in December and four additional academies scheduled for 2027.
chapters.title: Goodwin reports academy optimization and graduation numbers

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Our probation training academy has been strategically optimized from 5.1 months to 3.5 months, while maintaining compliance with the New York State training mandates and regulatory requirements.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So far this year, we have conducted two probation academies, graduating 57 officers with roughly another 50 candidates expected to graduate in December.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: In total, this amounts to almost 100 more offices joining the Department of Probation Family in 2026 when we need them the most.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Combined with four additional academies scheduled to be completed in 2027, my hope is that we will be almost fully staffed by the end of next year.

chapters.summary: Goodwin thanks Chair Brooks-Powers for attending academy graduations and Probation Week. She says the chair has helped celebrate the work of the small but mighty agency.
chapters.title: Goodwin thanks Chair Brooks-Powers for supporting probation officers

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: to take a moment to thank you, Chair Brooks-Powers, for your commitment to our offices.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Too often, the work of probation goes unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Since becoming chair, you have not only attended both academy graduations, but even joined our agency to celebrate Probation Week.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Thank you for seeing and celebrating the hard work and dedication of this small but mighty agency and its people.

chapters.summary: Goodwin says with staffing improving, DOP is returning to assigning caseloads according to risk. She says previous mixed caseloads led to lower-risk clients getting too much intervention and higher-risk clients too little, and DOP is reassessing cases to right-size them.
chapters.title: Goodwin describes right-sizing caseloads by risk level

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: With staffing and hiring trending positively, we could now return to another evidence-based practice, assigning caseloads according to risk or right-sizing caseloads.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Clients who engage in higher risk behavior require more attention, intervention, time, and resources.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Therefore, we continue to work towards ensuring that the offices supervising the highest risk behaviors have the fewest number of cases.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: When I returned to the agency, we found that previous policies have resulted in a mixed bag of caseloads.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Offices were overloaded from having to supervise a high number of cases, mixing low, medium, and high-risk behavior clients.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Not only is this poor practice from a workload perspective, but often results in lower-risk behavior getting too much intervention and high-risk behavior is not enough.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We reassured

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: assess the caseloads and right-size them according to risk level.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: A return to long-standing agency practice that our veteran offices are very familiar with and therefore should result in better outcomes for the people we serve.

chapters.summary: Goodwin says DOP cannot do the work alone and is rebuilding relationships with judges, service providers, and community organizations. She says DOP has met with judges to restore court liaison offices, paid overdue contracts, and reestablished NEON stakeholder groups.
chapters.title: Goodwin on rebuilding relationships with judges, providers, and NEON stakeholders

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Lastly, we know we cannot do this work alone.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Here at Probation, community is not only the neighborhoods our clients call home, but also the broader community of neighborhood-based organizations, businesses, nonprofits,

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: government agencies, judges, and other stakeholders who are key partners in this work.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Rebuilding those trusted relationships is not only the right thing to do, but necessary to ensure our clients have what they need to succeed.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Already this year, we have met with the judges to begin restoring our court liaison offices and family court.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We have paid long overdue and even elapsed contracts with struggling service providers.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We are rebuilding our Neighborhood Opportunity Networks, NEON model, by reestablishing our NEON stakeholder groups, ensuring community voice is part of community decision making.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Because when probation and the larger community are working together, anything is possible.

chapters.summary: Goodwin shares a success story of a probation client who completed a commercial driver's license certificate through Emerge Careers and the Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice. She says the client graduated with two job offers paying over $80,000 a year.
chapters.title: Goodwin highlights client CDL success with Emerge and MOCJ

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: For example, earlier this year, one of our probation clients broke the record for fastest completion of the commercial driver's license certificate.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: In partnership with Emerge Careers Next Mile program and the Mayor's Office of Criminal Justice, our client graduated with not one but two job offers paying over $80,000 a year.

chapters.summary: Goodwin says DOP supports the intent of Intro 1104 and that it generally matches current practice. She says probation provides young people and families a package of information, including a notice of rights, during family court intake, and looks forward to aligning the bill with the Family Court Act.
chapters.title: Goodwin supports Intro 1104 intent and describes current intake notice practice

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: A key part of our role is supporting young people and their families.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Is assuring that they have access to information about their rights and family court process.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Regarding Intro 1104, the department supports the intent of the bill and it generally matches our current practice.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: As part of intake process in family court,

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Probation provides the young person and their family with a package of information, including a notice of rights.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: While there are some details in Intro 1104 where we have recommendations, my team and I look forward to working with the council

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: to ensure that this bill aligns with the Family Court Act and best serves our young people and their families.

chapters.summary: Goodwin says proper staffing, right-sized caseloads, and strong relationships are fundamental to probation work. She says the department still has a way to go but she is proud of the work and dedication of DOP staff.
chapters.title: Goodwin concludes testimony on staffing, caseloads, and relationships

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Proper staffing, right-sized caseloads, and strong relationships are fundamental to the work we do.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And as you have heard, probation is all about focusing on what works.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Although we still have a way to go, I am beyond proud of the work.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And dedication so far this year from the people of this department.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Our client deserves

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: My team and I are pleased to answer any questions you have.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers thanks Goodwin for submitting testimony in time and says it helped her prepare questions. She acknowledges that Council Members Restler and Feliz have joined the hearing.
chapters.title: Chair thanks Commissioner and notes members present before questions

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I just want to publicly thank you for getting your testimony to me in time.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: While it was not the 24, 48 hours I was looking for, it still counts.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I was able to read your testimony while I was on the train in today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I feel like it's helpful because it helps me to reconfigure the questions we're going to ask to make sure that the conversation is meaningful.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I appreciate that, and I want to acknowledge the effort.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to also acknowledge that we've now been joined by council members, Ressler and Felice as well.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And we'll just jump into the questions.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what organizational changes DOP has implemented since January 2026 and what remains in development. Goodwin cites staffing and recruitment, risk-based caseload reassignment, rebuilt stakeholder relationships, NEON stakeholder groups, DOP Anchors data work, and evidence-based practices.
chapters.title: Chair asks about organizational changes since January 2026; Goodwin details staffing, caseloads, and data

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So regarding department leadership and organizational strategy, what organizational changes have been implemented since January 2026 and which remain in development?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: First is staffing and recruitment.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We have really focused more on getting the agency staffed up with probation officers, and by adding the probation officer training title

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: back to probation, we were able to really work with the different universities and their graduates to get them on board at probation.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We also looked at, reassessed all our cases, and

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: establish them in terms of their risk levels.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So now probation officers can focus on the lows, mediums, and highs, and it's not a mixed bag of cases.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: They also, it gives us an opportunity to lower the caseloads for the cases that require it, which is the highs and the mediums.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We also went out and started rebuilding our relationships with our stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I've met with the judges.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I've met with the borough presidents, judges, borough presidents, staff, clients.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We've been out there doing the work, and I'm proud of that.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We also reestablished our NEON stakeholders group, which now brings the community back into our NEONs, back into probation, and start informing the work that we do around NEON in terms of NEON sports, NEON arts, NEON Inspired.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We've been working real hard in that area.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And one of the things that probation put together is our

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Department of Probation Anchors, which is our data and technology, using information and technology to improve decision-making and identifying needs and opportunities and make our work more effective.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We look at strengthening client and community engagement, strengthening the relationships with the clients, families, and communities, including the strategic use of credible messengers and continued

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: evolution of the NEONs as community assets.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We are focusing on staff.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And team development and retention, investing in our people through strong relationships, professional development, support, accountability, and opportunities for growth.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And also, of course, number one, evidence-based and evidence-informed best practices, using research and evidence to guide what we do while continuously evaluating, learning, and adapting when the evidence is still developing.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how DOP measures whether changes are working and what metrics show. Goodwin says DOP is working with CUNY's Institute for State and Local Governance to build a framework and data points for evaluating community-based programs.
chapters.title: Chair asks how DOP measures changes; Goodwin cites CUNY ISLG framework

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And that's a good segue into my next question, which was going to be how the department is measuring whether these changes are working and what do those metrics show so far?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: One of the things I can say is that we are working with

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: CUNY's Institute for State and Local Governance on our framework to establish metrics and evaluate our community-based programs.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We also are focusing on building our own data points right now.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So we're in the middle of building this framework so we can really look at how we are governing ourselves at probation.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers pivots to staff vacancies and asks how many DOP currently has. Goodwin says there are 171 vacancies overall, with 134 in the probation officer title series.
chapters.title: Chair asks current vacancies; Goodwin reports 171 total and 134 probation officers

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to pivot to staff and vacancies recruitment and retention.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So how many vacancies does the department currently have across all titles and how many are in the probation officer title?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Right now we have 171 vacancies and 134 are in the probation officer title series.

chapters.title: Chair asks projected vacancies; Eusebio says DOP expects full staffing by mid-2027

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Now, the 171, is that inclusive of the two classes that have...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That number is already taken out of this.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But you project what the vacancy will be for next year?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because I know in your statement you had made a comment about that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So where do you project the vacancy to be at the end of next year again?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So for the record, Rob Lucevia, first deputy commissioner, we are currently looking to graduate 50 candidates in December.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We have several classes simultaneously coming up to next year, so we should be fully staffed at fiscal year 2017.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how many probation officers left and were hired over the past three fiscal years. Eusebio says about 388 people left the agency over three calendar years and notes the probation officer vacancy is down to 134.
chapters.title: Chair asks separations and hires over past three fiscal years; Eusebio reports 388 left

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many probation officers have left the department in each of the past three fiscal years, and how many have been hired during the same periods?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So report that we have was about 388 folks left the agency within those three calendar years.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We, as indicated here, our vacancy is down to 134 in the probation officer series.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: And as I indicated earlier, we have a class of 50 graduating in December.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So we should be, obviously, with the organic attrition, we should be in line with our staffing by mid-year 27.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks the primary reasons probation officers have been leaving. Goodwin cites competition from other law enforcement agencies, salaries, retirements, and unbalanced work-life schedules, and says she changed schedules to improve retention.
chapters.title: Chair asks why officers leave; Goodwin cites competition, salaries, retirements, and schedules

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And what do you feel the primary reasons are that the probation officers have been leaving?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: It varies in so many different areas, but one is it's very competitive out there.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Two is salaries.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We're competing with other law enforcement agencies.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And three is people is retiring.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: You know, we had a lot of people have been at probation for a long time and over 25 years or more.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Just at this table is over 100 and something years of experience.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And we're still here fighting the fight.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So it varies.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: But hopefully, you know.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I did some changes in that area because even their schedules, they didn't have a balanced work-life experience.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And so when I got back, that was one of the first things I did was change their schedule.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And so they can have spend more time with their family.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And really help themselves, you know.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And we have a lot of re-experience at probation in terms of doing a lot of work with the probation officer.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: By the same token, it should be noted under the leadership of Community of Goodwin, we have upward of nearly 30 people who have returned just because, you know, the interest in the work, the passion for our community and for the work that we do.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether DOP uses data to compare wages with other law enforcement agencies and make the case for higher entry-level pay. Goodwin says her HR director tracks retention, projected retirements, and hiring needs to stay balanced.
chapters.title: Chair asks about using wage data to compete; Goodwin says HR tracks retirements and hiring

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'd like to acknowledge we've been joined by Councilmember Caban as well.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Well, just staying in line with this, because there are certain, I feel like, jobs in New York City that, you know,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: deserve a lot more in terms of their wages.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I'm curious, now that you're looking at using different metrics and data, as it pertains to wages for probation officers to attract more talent,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Have you begun using data to, I guess, compare and contrast to other law enforcement agencies that you're in competition with to present and

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: make the case for higher wages for the entry-level folks coming in?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We are looking at that.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: You know, my HR director is constantly looking at our retention, who's like set to retire, and also making sure that we are matching the

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: possible people who are going to retire that we're matching it that we are hiring even more so we can stay balanced so yes we are looking at what those numbers are looking like in terms of who's

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: projected to leave and who what we need to do to make sure we stay on course.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers says the council should work with DOP before the next fiscal cycle to understand what funding is needed to attract talent. She says keeping people on probation rather than in carceral settings is a shared goal.
chapters.title: Chair urges budget talks on funding to attract probation talent

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: As we get prepared to go into the next fiscal cycle, it would be great to work in advance of that to understand, like, what type of funding the department would need to better attract talent to come in.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because obviously we're looking to try and get as many people that are eligible on the path to probation as opposed to having them in a carceral setting unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so if there's a way that the council can help to support that effort, it'll be great to start having those conversations as well.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how long it takes on average to fill a probation officer vacancy. Assistant Commissioner Xenia Melendez says DOP provisionally posts positions, interviews within two weeks, and moves candidates to medical, psychological, and background checks within about a month.
chapters.title: Chair asks how long it takes to fill a probation officer vacancy; Melendez describes month-long process

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In terms of timing, how long does it take on average for a probation officer vacancy to be filled?

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: My name is Xenia Melendez, Assistant Commissioner of Human Resources.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: You can go closer to the table.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: She was sworn in.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: She raised her hand.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Xenia Melendez, Assistant Commissioner of Human Resources.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Just depending on the title.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: So, for example, as Commissioner Goodwin indicated, she did reinstate the probation officer trainee position.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: So we would provisionally post the position.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Within two weeks, we get a numerous amount of candidates who are interested.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: We interview.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: I'd say within a month, we'd have candidates who are moving on to the next pre-employment phase, which includes medical, psychological, and background investigations.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: So within a month, we can have candidates who are already moving forward for the position.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers confirms that candidates move to the academy after about a month and that the academy is now 3.5 months, down from 5.1. Melendez says academy trainees are paid, receive benefits, and the time counts toward probation service.
chapters.title: Chair confirms academy length, pay, and benefits with Melendez

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So it takes about a month to get all that information.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Then they get put on the track for the academy?

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then academy is how long again?

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: 3.5 months.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: 3.5 months, down from 5.1.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: See, I read it on the train.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I told y'all.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: This is how it's helpful because, see, we have a real conversation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay, and so now it's 3.5 months.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So that's like...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Less than half a year, you could be into like a...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: career path at that point.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: We currently have an academy class that's in the academy now, and we're gearing for our December academy as we speak.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And the academy to get paid also?

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The full amount?

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: With benefits?

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And it's a part of the probation time frame?

utterances.speaker: Xenia Melendez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I just want to have it on the record for those who's watching.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: They may be looking for a career change or something.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how the academy is structured between classroom and field training and how DOP arrived at its length. Director of Training Jason Torres says the academy has three phases, with field training and hands-on training in later stages after state and regulatory requirements.
chapters.title: Chair asks about academy structure; Torres explains three phases and field training

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: For the academy, how is the academy currently structured between classroom and field training?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How did the department arrive at the length of the training?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I know in the testimony it was stated that it's following the state guidance, but just wanting to understand that a little bit better as well.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: Good morning, council members.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't think you were smiling.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: Jason Torres, director of training.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: My mom, I swear you in.

utterances.speaker: Jahari Frazier
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Jahari Frazier
utterances.text: Torres, do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and to answer, thank you, and to answer council member questions honestly?

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Jahari Frazier
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jahari Frazier
utterances.text: Now you may continue.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: Good morning again, Councilman.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: Jason Torres, Director of Training.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: So our approach to this has been strategically optimized from 5.1 to 3.5 months.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: They go through several phases.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: There are three phases that they have, phase one, phase two, phase three of the academy.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: A portion of that, which would be the latter stages of the academy, is where they get field training.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: They also get hands-on training as well.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: So once they complete their state and regulatory requirements, then they move on to different phases.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: The last phase would be inclusive of that.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how the current academy structure affects new officers' readiness. Torres says DOP optimized the academy by focusing on core requirements, supplementing them with additional training, and reducing field time because graduates receive hands-on training on the job.
chapters.title: Chair asks how academy changes affect readiness; Torres says core requirements plus added training

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And how has the current structure of the academy affected the new officers' readiness?

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: By strategically optimizing it, what we did was get down to the core requirements that are needed.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: With addition to those core requirements, we supplement those requirements with additional training as well.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: Some of the training that we saw before, there was an extended period of field training out in the field itself.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: So what we did was we reduced the time that they were out in the field to provide more training for them because they were going to get hands-on training as soon as they graduate from there.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: So it was all about optimizing and planning ahead to ensure that we increase the level of training modalities, but also the effectiveness of it when they are operational.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what training new officers receive after the academy, including for vulnerable youth. Eusebio, Goodwin, and Ruggieri describe continuous training, borough onboarding, shadowing, refreshers, and at least 21 mandatory training hours per year.
chapters.title: Chair asks about post-academy training for vulnerable youth; DOP describes ongoing onboarding

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And what training do new officers receive after graduating from the academy?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is there any specific training related to support in vulnerable youth, for example, that's done?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I know in like PD, they have training modules that they can do, but they don't often get time to do it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I'm curious in terms of how probation approaches training after the academy has completed.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Jason Torres
utterances.text: I'm going to defer over to the deputy commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So probation as a practice is an ongoing, we training ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: In fact, even those that have been in the job a long time know

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: that best practice requires that we continuously honing in our skills, whether it's motivation interviewing, whether it's stages of change, whether anything else that relates to what's best practice in the field, we constantly in that quest.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So to say that someone is fully trained, it means that we continuously look into what's going to make us do better in terms of engaging our clients so they can be on a path to meeting the goals.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: What happens once they leave the academy, they are onboarded by their, each borough assistant commissioner onboards the new people.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So that means teaching them about setting goals, case management, how to supervise whatever risk they're going to receive.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: They do, they have to learn how to run a rap sheet.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: They have to learn e-justice.

utterances.speaker: Tina Ruggieri
utterances.text: Tina Ruggieri, Deputy Commissioner for the Operations.

utterances.speaker: Tina Ruggieri
utterances.text: As part of the onboarding, they're shadowing.

utterances.speaker: Tina Ruggieri
utterances.text: They shadow the officers, you know, once they graduate from the academy as well.

utterances.speaker: Tina Ruggieri
utterances.text: So, and as First Deputy Commissioner says, there's also refreshers, trainings throughout for the existing officers who are veterans.

utterances.speaker: Tina Ruggieri
utterances.text: So it's an ongoing training.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Anything else you wanted to add, Commissioner?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Well, other than the practice itself requires that everyone has X amount, we do 21 at least, mandatory 21 hours of training every year, and usually focus on the work that the person is sort of conducting out there in the field.

chapters.summary: Council Member Morano asks whether high-risk individuals were receiving insufficient supervision under the previous mixed-caseload system. Goodwin says they were supervised but did not always get the right dosage of intervention, and says the mixed-bag practice lasted about three years.
chapters.title: Morano questions DOP on high-risk caseloads and insufficient supervision

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to yield.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I have more questions, but I'm going to allow my colleagues to ask their questions, starting with Councilmember Marano, followed by Councilmember Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, thank you for your testimony, and thank you for your four decades of service to the city and to the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Appreciate it very much.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I was particularly interested in your testimony because you said your department's organizational strategy can be summarized in two words, what works.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And that's a great philosophy for all of us in city government.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I think my concern is whether we're actually measuring what works, particularly when it comes to public safety.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: There was one thing in your testimony that really jumped out at me.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You said that under the previous...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: system, your officers had a mixed bag of caseloads, which resulted in people exhibiting lower risk behavior, receiving too much intervention, and people exhibiting high risk behavior, receiving not enough.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Obviously, I think we'd all recognize that's backwards.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I appreciate the department's admission on that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So are you telling us that individuals your own department considered high risk weren't receiving the level of supervision they should be receiving?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I'm going to say that they were receiving supervision, but one of the things that concerns me is making sure that they are really getting the interventions that they needed.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I think that when you have a mixed bag of cases, you pick a lane and you stay in it.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: You're not giving the right amount of dosage to the people, and that really concerned me.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do we know how long that was happening, the insufficient amount of dosage, let's say?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And more importantly, do we know whether anyone committed a serious violent crime while receiving less supervision than the department's own risk assessment called for?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: In terms of the mixed bag, I think it's been about three years.

chapters.summary: Morano asks what is behind the reported 50% increase in juvenile rearrests and what share involved violent offenses. Deputy Commissioner Stacey Dessimore cites staffing shortages and officers carrying mixed risk levels, and says DOP is aligning units by risk and lowering high-risk caseloads.
chapters.title: Morano asks about 50% juvenile rearrest increase; Dessimore cites staffing and unit alignment

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: However, I don't know of anyone involved in any high crime or violent crime or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The committee report indicated that juvenile rearrests increased by 50%.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's very concerning to me, not just because it means young people are getting into more trouble, but because every additional crime potentially means another innocent New Yorker has been victimized.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Can you tell us what's behind that 50% increase, including the time period it covers, and what percentage of those rearrests involved violent offenses?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Good morning, Stacey Decimor, Deputy Commissioner for Juvenile Operations.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So as you know, we all know that the juvenile arrest numbers have increased.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: But I do want to say that since this commissioner has been here, our arrest rate has started to decrease, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And one of the things that she talked about is making sure that we are supervising the young people one size fits one, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we are targeting those young people as soon as they get placed on probation.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We are making sure that we are connecting with their circle of influence, who is important to that young person, who is able to help navigate the system with that young person.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We are also making sure that we are really sharing that load with our community-based organizations, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: It's a collective approach, and it's a partnership.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We also know that we want to make sure that we have the right staff and enough staff, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So that is why we are staffing up to make sure that we have enough officers for those high-risk caseloads.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Currently, we have, out of the 43 supervision officers in juvenile, we have 18 that are strictly monitoring those cases.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So we have some branches that have gun units, you know, for those that are on probation for firearms.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We have those that are in level four, which is your highest level of supervision.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We want to make sure that they have the lower caseload attacking them.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: and making sure that they're getting the services.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: It's not where we want to be.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We understand it's a challenge, and we are always about public safety, and we are working diligently to lower that arrest rate.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well, no, we all want the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I wanted to add, since my appointment has been nine months, and so just like adult, juvenile also, we went back and reassessed all those cases and separated them out so we can focus

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: intently on who needs the most intervention.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether the CDL success story is representative and what percentage of participants complete employment and rehabilitation programs. Eusebio says DOP sees a 60-70% completion rate but wants better tracking, and Goodwin says CUNY ISLG will help evaluate outcomes.
chapters.title: Morano asks about employment program completion rates; Eusebio cites 60-70%

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let me ask you about one of the success stories that you mentioned involving a probation client who completed commercial driver's license training and received two job offers paying more than $80,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And that's terrific.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I'd love to hear more success stories like that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I also think taxpayers are entitled to know whether these are isolated success stories or representative of broader results.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Of the people participating in your employment and rehab programs, what percentage successfully complete them, find employment, and then avoid a new arrest?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Well, obviously, we're looking here today, obviously, so we're not going to speak to the past, at least under the leadership of Commissioner Goodwin.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We are encouraged by the fact that we're seeing a decrease all around in terms of things, people engaging in negative outcomes, right?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: To say who is completing the program and who is getting it, we see a 60%, 70% completion rate as it relates to programming.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We want to do better in terms of keeping track of that.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So that's part of the framework that we're sort of building to sort of be able to tell you apple to apple.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Obviously, we don't have a cohort, so it's fluid.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We get new cases every day, but we're encouraged by what we've seen thus far.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And that's the reason why we're working with CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And, you know, I, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I-S-L-G.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I always get that.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I-S-L-G.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And so we can start looking at that and we can come and report more in terms of, and also hiring different consultants to look at what we're doing

chapters.summary: Council Member Restler says DOP was badly mismanaged under the previous administration and asks how DOP will restore programs that were cut, including Impact, Next Steps, Arches, AIM, and ICM. Goodwin says DOP may not bring back old programs but will develop new ones and is working with community organizations.
chapters.title: Restler criticizes prior DOP mismanagement and asks about restoring eliminated programs

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: and we can get a better read and evaluation about our work.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Councilmember, if you have more questions, I can bring you up after Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thanks so much, Chair Brooke Powers, and it's great to be with you here at this committee and great to be with the leadership of the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Over the last four years, I received many, many dozens of complaints.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Lots were anonymous of cronyism, corruption, incompetence at the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I will tell you of all of the agencies that I think were badly mismanaged during the previous administration, none more so than the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so the scale of the turnaround that you are charged with is greater than any other commissioner in city government.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's really tragic to me what the previous administration did because over your 40-year career, the Department of Probation had been a model of reform and innovation in city government.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: From the Bloomberg to the de Blasio administrations, we had great leaders who were doing really compelling and innovative things.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And that all came to a really harsh stop in recent years.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I'm heartened by your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm impressed by your plan to be fully staffed up at the end of next year.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, it takes– when somebody hollows out an agency, when somebody–

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: encourages, when somebody, I think, does such a poor job of leading an agency and people leave en masse and programs are eliminated, it takes time to build it back up.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It doesn't happen in a day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really want to focus my questions today around some of the programs that Commissioner Holmes eliminated and get an understanding of where they are and how you're repairing and restoring.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm particularly concerned about youth incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: During the Adams administration, we went from about 150 kids in our juvenile detention facilities to well over 370.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That number more than doubled.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And part of the problem is that the Department of Probation was nowhere to be found and was not a partner.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We heard from leaders across city government that they could no longer rely on DOP.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so we're keen to see how DOP is now stepping up to help solve these problems.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Under the past administration, there were over $5 million in cuts to evidence-based programs that serve at-risk young adults, cuts of $700,000 to the impact program, $2.6 million to next steps, $1.6 million to arches,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: and DOP stopped making referrals to the AIM program, the Advocate Intervene Mentor Program.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The Intensive Community Monitor Program, ICM, was reportedly hollowed out, and probation officers were joining ARCHES meetings, which goes against every best practice that I've ever come across.

chapters.summary: Goodwin says DOP is looking at new programming, including partnerships like Emerge, and will issue white papers with community organizations. She says programs should allow clients to finish certifications at their own pace and explore fields like AI and IT.
chapters.title: Goodwin outlines plans for new programs and white papers

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So what I'd really love is if you and your team today could help us walk through

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: what are the plans to restore each of those programs or alternatives that you're pursuing so that we can get DOP to be making a difference again to help keep young adults out of juvenile detention.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I want to say that it is our goal to be innovative and bold and bring probation back to its glory.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: The second is that the programs that are no longer at probation,

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I've met with a lot of different community-based organizations, and what I've said to them is that we may not be able to bring it back, but what we can do is develop new ones, older ones.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And we have...

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Enough experience to learn about what worked and what didn't and what we can add to programming.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So we are looking at putting out different white papers, working with the organizations to like bring back different innovative programs such as working like with the program like Emerge.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: The clients have a

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: opportunity to work at their own pace.

chapters.summary: Restler says there are 352 young adults in juvenile detention and DOP needs to help drive down incarceration. He asks about current DOP policy on officers carrying guns after Commissioner Holmes required every uniformed officer to carry one.
chapters.title: Restler underscores juvenile detention urgency and asks about gun policy

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: You know, it's not like you have to finish between, you got four months to finish this program.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: A lot of the programs that we're really looking at is making sure that the client can finish whatever certification, but it's done at their pace.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And we're looking to look for, you know,

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: you know, anything in AI, IT, we're looking at a plethora of different programming to bring back to probation.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I would just underscore the urgency because, you know, I think as of Friday, Councilmember Stevens told me we have 352 young adults in our juvenile detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We do not have capacity.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I've heard a lot from the Mndani administration about how they're renovating spaces and creating more beds for people.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I have heard less about how we're driving down incarceration.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And we need DOP to step up and be a real partner there.

chapters.summary: Eusebio says DOP has moved away from requiring all uniformed officers to carry guns and is determining who should be armed. McKenzie says he helped architect the prior policy, DOP is returning to it, and a draft should go to the executive team and union before being shared with the council.
chapters.title: Eusebio and McKenzie describe return to prior gun policy and draft written policy

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm going to get cut off, so I want to ask one more question, which is,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Guns.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Commissioner Holmes insisted that every uniformed officer carry a gun.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What is the current policy of the Department of Probation as it relates to guns?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So obviously we have moved away from some of the policies that didn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Part of this is we are in tangent working with the whole team working in what makes sense, who should carry and shouldn't carry.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We have made policies that support the people that needs to be, you know, obviously given the nature of our work that needs to be armed, will remain armed.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: But by and large, the agency is not mandating folks that are in known, you know, enforcement unit to carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is there a new written policy that can be shared with us?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We, what stage is the policy?

chapters.summary: Restler thanks Goodwin and McKenzie and says he looks forward to DOP restoring its former reputation. McKenzie thanks Restler and says DOP looks forward to his support.
chapters.title: Restler closes by welcoming back Goodwin and McKenzie

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Good day, Wayne McKenzie, Deputy Commissioner for Legal and External Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: I was actually one of the architects of the former policy under the Sheraldi administration.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: So we're returning to that and we're hoping within the next week or so.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: We'll actually have a draft for our exec team to approve, and at which point we'll then have the union obviously weigh in, and we'd be ready to share it with the council.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We would really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I just, you know, as I close, just want to say.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Welcome back to city government, Commissioner Goodwin, Deputy Commissioner McKenzie, and many others, you know, and look forward to you all restoring the Department of Probation to its glory.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Morano asks what specific public safety outcomes New Yorkers should expect in a year, such as fewer rearrests or better compliance. Goodwin says she wants to look at how programming informs client outcomes and says DOP is building its metrics.
chapters.title: Morano asks what public safety outcomes should improve in a year

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: And as always, we look forward to your support.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Councilmember Morano.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I don't necessarily have anything else.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Just the one– I'll ask one– make one comment and I'll ask one other question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I recognize that we want to focus on the statistics over the last nine months because that's a reflection of what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I also think–

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: for some of the reasons my colleagues have alluded to, it's also important to look back and see what the differences were based on before you guys took over as compared to now.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'll ask one final question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony did focus on what's working internally.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: at the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If we're sitting here a year from now, what specific public safety outcomes should New Yorkers expect to have improved as a result of the organizational changes that you guys have made?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Will we see fewer rearrests, fewer violent offenses committed by individuals under supervision, better compliance among high-risk probationers, something else?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When we do this a year from now, what can we go back and look at as a measure of the department's success?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I think you answered the question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Well, anything I'm missing?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: One of the things I think I really want to look at, too, is how program is informing our outcomes in terms of changing the lives of our clients.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So I would add that to the list.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how many juvenile cases were eligible for adjustment in fiscal year 2026 and how many were adjusted. Dessimore says about 9,000 cases came through intake and about 1,400 were adjusted, and says the adjustment rate is not where she wants it.
chapters.title: Chair asks about juvenile adjustment cases; Dessimore reports 9,000 intake and 1,400 adjusted

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So it's a lot that we are putting together in terms of what our metrics is actually going to look like.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sticking with juvenile probation adjustment and diversion, how many cases were eligible for adjustment in fiscal year 2026?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And how many were actually adjusted?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Good morning again, Stacey Dessimore.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We had approximately 9,000 cases that came through intake and about 1,400 that were adjusted.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: What is eligible for adjustment depends on the charges, depends on the circumstance of the case, and that's the process of an intake probation officer is to determine the eligibility and the suitability of the case to be diverted from court.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: I know that our adjustment rate is not where we want it to be, and that is something that I am going to be working with my team.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We had started looking at the cases.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we have the right staff in place to be able to effectively

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: assess a case and looking at that young person as a whole and seeing what that young person's strengths are, but also what are some of the challenges so that we can determine why can't we divert this case from court.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We want to divert as many suitable and possible cases from further court involvement, right?

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how the adjustment rate compares to prior years and administrations. Dessimore says she is reviewing why cases were not adjusted, notes designated felonies cannot be diverted without court approval, and plans training and retraining for juvenile staff by March.
chapters.title: Chair asks how adjustment compares to prior years; Dessimore discusses eligibility and training

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We want to give that young person an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So that is something that I'm committed to with my team to make sure that we get to a place where we're used to.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: I mean, I've been around, and I know when the adjustment rate was very high at 41.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And I think that we are going to set a goal of 20% for the next fiscal year to reach.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: You waited in my next question, so it seems like we were sharing notes, it feels like, today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But I was going to ask, how does it compare to prior years and prior administrations?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
