utterances.text: So it sounds like there has been some significant change.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We have to really, what I plan on doing and what I've started doing is just looking at why we made certain decisions, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And we want to look at what were the class and charges, again, what was eligible.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And, of course, you know, with the eligibility, that relates to the charge.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We cannot.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Divert a designated felony case, those serious charges, without the approval of the court.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So then we want to make sure that those that are suitable and eligible, what is making us determine that they're not and we have to refer them to further court process.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what services are available to young people whose cases are adjusted. Dessimore describes mentoring, Saturday programs, employment, school support, parent coaches, and wraparound funds tailored to youth interests and victim considerations.
chapters.title: Chair asks what services are available for adjusted cases; Dessimore lists supports

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So I want to look at how the staff is assessing cases, again, making sure that we have enough staff in those key places and making sure that they are trained and we are doing

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: just overall in juvenile operations, we are going to be doing training and retraining of every staff and hopefully by March of next year, everyone will be in a good position.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And I'm happy that we have more staff coming out of the classes so that we can bulk up in those areas that are important because probation is the front door and we are, you know, we want to be able to

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: do what is necessary, help those young people connect with community-based organizations, services, whatever they need, so that they don't come through our door again.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And that's the whole point of it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What services are available to young people whose cases are adjusted?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So we have, it depends, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Again, we want to know what that young person, their interests are, what is the nature of the offense, and try to target those services and interventions based on that, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We also want to take into account if there's a victim on the case, what their position is or what their feeling is to try to sort of make them whole, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We have mentoring for the young people.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We also have Saturday programs.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We also have employment.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We also support that young person with school if there's any educational needs.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We are making sure that we are addressing that.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And we also have services for the parent, right, because it's a challenging process.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: I speak to parents all the time, and they are fearful, right, of the process, and they're fearful of their child and what this means for them, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So we have parent support and parent coaches for every parent from the beginning of intake throughout the probation process to make sure that.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: They have someone to help navigate the system.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So whatever the young person needs, and if there's something that they're interested in, you know, we want to make sure that we're targeting.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether DOP is aware that judges may be more inclined to grant early termination motions filed by probation. Goodwin says DOP is looking at all eligible cases and that the early discharge practice has been restored.
chapters.title: Chair asks about early termination; Goodwin says practice is back

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: If the young person wants to do boxing, if the young person wants to do...

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: creative writing.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: If the young person is interested in cosmetology, we want to make sure that we are targeting that.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We have wraparound funds for that to make sure we get what the young person needs.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Pivoting to early termination of probation, we have been told that judges may be more inclined to grant motions for early termination of probation when those motions are filed by the Department of Probation.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how many times DOP has filed motions to terminate probation early since the new administration and how that compares to prior administrations. Eusebio says DOP is returning to the practice but does not have exact numbers yet and will provide them.
chapters.title: Chair asks how many early termination motions filed; Eusebio lacks exact numbers

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is this something that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And I'm glad to say that probation is now looking at all of our cases that are eligible for us to do early discharges.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I know it was a cease in practice, but I can report that it's back.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And since the start of this administration, how many times has the department filed a motion to terminate someone's probation early?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And do you know how that number compares to previous administrations?

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what factors determine whether DOP files for early termination. Eusebio and Goodwin cite public safety, mitigating factors, employment, stable housing, family stability, program completion, and no rearrest.
chapters.title: Chair asks factors for early termination; Eusebio and Goodwin list criteria

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So obviously we're coming back to that practice.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Currently, I don't have the exact numbers, but we're encouraged by the fact that our philosophy is aligning with our value.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We are definitely going to be coming back to this body with numbers, concrete numbers, to inform that practice where we are.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Better yet, you can just send it to us in writing before the week is out.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That would be great.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What factors go into determining whether to file a motion for early termination?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So every case, we assess everyone who is on probation.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Part of that assessment is making sure that we have addressed any, you know, mitigating factors that any concerns for public safety.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Obviously, that's what we're looking for before we put someone through the, you know, submission of early discharges.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We're looking at the whole person, you know, are they employed?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Are they staying in a rest free?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Are they, you know, doing things positive, reengaging with the family?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We're also making sure that they know where to turn to if they ever need support.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: NEON is one of the resources that we heavily rely on.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Make sure they know that if they ever find themselves in need of any support, they can still come back to probation regardless of whether they are on probation or not.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And I would add, in terms of what we look at for early discharges is making sure that the person hasn't been rearrested.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks why general counsel might oppose early termination when an assigned officer and supervisor agree. McKenzie says under the current administration every early discharge is assessed on its merits and there should be no blanket objections.
chapters.title: Chair asks about disconnect between officers and general counsel on early termination

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We look at to see if they have steady employment.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We look at their family dynamics and their situation and it's stable.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We look at if they completed either high school or vocational program.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So it's a number of things that we look at that we can inform the court that this person is doing well and they are no longer a threat to themselves or the community.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We have heard that in situation when a person's assigned probation officer, when a person's assigned probation officer and that officer's supervisor are in agreement about early termination, that the department's

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: general counsel may still oppose or take.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: No position on such determination.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What causes the disconnect between the position of an assigned officer and a general counsel?

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: So I'm not going to speak to the practices of any previous administration.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: I can say under this current administration, every early discharge is assessed on its merits.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: So there should be no blanket.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Objection from the Office of General Counsel in this regard.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: And in fact,

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: We'd like to encourage early discharges when people are entitled to it.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So, so far you haven't had to contend with that, but you're.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thoughts are that you don't see.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: We've had one situation where I had to issue some clarification around certain types of cases.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: And that clarification has been that every case should be judged on its own merits.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: There's no blanket objections.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I hear you about not having a blanket determination.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: However, what I'm asking is if there is an assigned officer and their supervisor that's saying one thing,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What would cause a disconnect with the general counsel to be in opposition of that determination from someone who is dealing more regularly with the individual?

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: There should be none.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: We should be guided by the recommendations of operations.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: There are certain legal factors, for example, in the law for someone to be eligible.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether officers are told ahead of time if general counsel may oppose or take no position on early termination. McKenzie says supervision officers drive the process, general counsel reviews for legal eligibility, and officers are counseled on any legal reasons.
chapters.title: Chair asks if officers know legal eligibility issues; McKenzie explains review process

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: And if there was some disconnect there, that would be...

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Right now, it's generally driven by policy.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: And I can tell you the policy is there is no blanket objections.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And staying in the same line of questioning, are the officers made aware ahead of time that the general counsel may oppose or express no opinion on early termination?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And you raise a valid point, right, because there may be something legally that may prevent that individual from being eligible.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: For this discharge.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so are the officers made aware before they even say, I think client X should have an early discharge?

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand because generally speaking, it's the supervision officers who are driving that process and general counsel should be doing a review.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers pivots to Intro 1104 and asks what information DOP currently provides to youth and parents before an intake interview. Dessimore says DOP provides a notice of rights, goes over the process, and now has court liaison officers give notices to families in cases removed from youth part.
chapters.title: Chair asks what DOP provides before intake; Dessimore describes notice of rights

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: And so if there is a legal reason, then obviously they're going to counsel the officers about the legal reason.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: If there is a strong...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So you've just answered me.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay, good.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Pivoting to intro 1104, my bill.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner, for your sentiments on the bill.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to having more conversations around it, but just had a few questions for the record.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What information does the department currently provide to young people and their parents or guardians before an intake interview?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So every parent and young person that comes to intake, we provide them with a notice of rights.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And then when the officer meets with the family, they go over the process.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: One thing that I did put into place is that for those

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: cases that are being removed from youth park, I've had the CLOs now keep copies of those notice of rights to give out to the family just in case they are not participating in the intake.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: At least they have those notice of rights so that they can review and have it before they even come over to the cases being removed over the family court.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So it's a process.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: It's whatever the parent has, whatever question we go through, this is a possibility that can happen based on

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: the circumstance of the case.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We're making sure we interview this person.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We try to gather information on the school.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what resources, training, or procedural changes DOP would need for Intro 1104. McKenzie says much of the bill aligns with DOP business practices and the Family Court Act, but DOP has recommendations, such as changing the adult term 'PSI' to fit family court.
chapters.title: Chair asks what changes Intro 1104 requires; McKenzie says it aligns with practice

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We try to gather information on how the young person is functioning within the community.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: All those things, and to let them know this is what we're taking into consideration when we're making a determination.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We also let them know just that the process is voluntary, right, and that they don't have to participate if they don't want to.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: But we do give them the notice in hand, but we also have a conversation once we sit with them in person.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What resources, staff training, or procedural changes would the department need to implement in show 1104?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What resources, staff training, or procedural changes would the department need to implement in Tro 1104?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So what changes would you need to do in order to be in compliance with this local law?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What is intro?

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: I don't know if we require any procedural trainings.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: A lot of what's in 1104.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Changes, not trainings.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Changes.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: A lot of what's in 1104 already aligns with much of our business practices and notices that we're required to give.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: By the Family Court Act.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Now, there may be certain recommendations that we have that we think can bring 1104 more in alignment with our business practices and the wordings of, for example, the Family Court Act.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether officers are adequately trained to explain statutory protections and governance statements during intake. McKenzie says training includes legal aspects taught by attorneys.
chapters.title: Chair asks if officers are trained to explain protections; McKenzie cites attorney training

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: As an example, 1104 refers to PSIs.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: And PSIs is something that's a phrase that's used in the adult context, but not in the family court context.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: And so we really look forward to working with you and your team to better align this bill.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Because as the commissioner says, it has our support.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether a standardized notice could help officers explain the process consistently. McKenzie says DOP believes it would.
chapters.title: Chair asks if standardized notice would help; McKenzie agrees

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Excuse me.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what information young people and families most need when they first interact with probation. McKenzie says the process is stressful and parent coaches can better explain the process and guide families through it.
chapters.title: Chair asks what families most need at first contact; McKenzie cites parent coaches

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Are offices adequately trained to explain the statutory protections, governance statements made during intake?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is there a training module in terms of how they should?

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: I think a number of us can answer that question, but part of the training module does include training by the attorneys on various legal aspects.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do you think that a standardized notice could further help the officers explain the process consistently?

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: We believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And in your estimation, what information do young people and families most need when they first interact with probation?

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: So I think what's needed the most is something that we may not actually be able to legislate, right?

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers notes that Council Members Salaam and Brewer have joined the hearing. She pivots to questions about court liaison officers and family court coordination.
chapters.title: Chair recognizes Salam and Brewer, pivots to court liaison officers

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Anytime you've got someone interacting with the criminal legal process at the beginning, there's a significant amount of stress.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: So, for example, in the juvenile context, I think one way we can do a better job is if we engage more.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Is it the parent coaches?

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how many court liaison officers DOP currently employs. Dessimore says DOP has 13 total, with eight for family court and five for youth part, and still needs one more for Manhattan and additional family court coverage in Queens and the Bronx.
chapters.title: Chair asks how many court liaison officers DOP employs; Dessimore reports 13

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: That is that's they're explaining the process and they're holding the individual by the hand and leading them through the process.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Just want to recognize we've been joined by council members Salam and Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to pivot to court liaison officers and family court coordination.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many court liaison officers does the department currently employ?

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how many court liaison officers are assigned to each borough and family court location. Dessimore lists coverage in the Bronx, Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Staten Island, including a hybrid CLO covering youth part and family court on Staten Island.
chapters.title: Chair asks CLO assignments by borough; Dessimore details coverage

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So I'm happy to say that we are staffing up in that area, and we have a total of 13.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: There's eight for family court, and we are staffing up the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We have five, and we need a total of six, so we need one more for Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We can use one more, though, for a family court in Queens and one more for a family court in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We'll send the job postings to the committee members.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: We'll make sure we put them out also.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I guess you answered the next question, which is how many court liaison officers are assigned to each borough.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And family court location.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: It's one for family court and one for youth part.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what responsibilities court liaison officers currently perform. Dessimore says youth part CLOs track arraignments, removals to family court, ICM cases, and court updates, while family court CLOs provide background, risk level, ATD information, and progress reports.
chapters.title: Chair asks CLO responsibilities; Dessimore describes youth part and family court roles

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: For the Bronx, we have two in family court.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And beginning on November 2nd, we will have two in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And then in Manhattan, we have two in family court.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And then in Brooklyn, we have three in family court, and we have one in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And in Staten Island, we have a hybrid where the CLO covers the youth part and family court.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What responsibilities do court liaison officers currently perform?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We'll start with the youth part, and I will say that the judges are very pleased that they have the CLOs back.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So for the youth part, the CLO is responsible for tracking any arraignment

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: for the purpose of whether or not the young person is going to be removed to family court and making sure that they have all the necessary information and documents to forward to their colleagues at intake.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Also, they track any case where the judge is placing a young person on an ICM or voluntary services.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And then they also provide the updates for the courts in all parties.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: In all parties when the young person appears at the adjournments.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And any information that the court, any questions they will answer that the court has with regards to those young people that may be on ICM or those cases that are being removed.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: They also speak to the families as the cases are being removed to family court to give them this information.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Of course, and also now the notice of rights.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks how DOP coordinates with the Administration for Children's Services, the Law Department, and defense counsel on juvenile cases. Dessimore describes coordination with ACS for detention releases, intake, arraignment, and weekend and evening arraignment coverage.
chapters.title: Chair asks how DOP coordinates with ACS, Law Dept, and defense counsel

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And then for the family court, so they are there available at arraignment.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So when the young person is arraigned on a new charge, they're there to provide the court with some background information and also let the court know what risk level they are to determine what

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: ATD they may be appropriate for available to that young person.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: They also stand up and provide information with regards to the investigations report and any progress report that is given to the court and all parties.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Any question that the judge may have in regards to how that young person who may be on probation, how they're functioning and they have additional questions that may not be

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: in the progress report, the CLO is there to facilitate that information and just be a conduit for the court and for probation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And how does the department coordinate with the Administration for Children's Services, the Law Department, and Defense Counsel on juvenile cases?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So I think we, of course, coordinate, I guess, with regards to ACS.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: It's, you know, for those young people that may be in detention and being released to probation or during the intake phase and at arraignment.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So, of course, you know, we have the team of officers that are coordinated with ACS who do weekend and evening arraignment for detention and intake.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what challenges remain in coordinating probation services with family court. Dessimore says some boroughs need more staff and one or two more CLOs, but she meets regularly with courts and judges to keep communication open.
chapters.title: Chair asks remaining family court coordination challenges; Dessimore cites staffing

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And what challenges remain in coordinating probation services with family court?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: I think, again, we probably need some boroughs maybe need a little bit more staff and one or two more CLOs just to be available for the court.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: I meet with the courts regularly, so we have that great open communication.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: I met with the Bronx judges, so we just talk about any issues and concerns.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So it's just making sure that they're readily available and that the information is flowing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Council Member Salaam asks about the current vacancy count and hiring targets to close the probation officer gap. Goodwin says DOP has 171 vacancies overall, 134 in the probation officer series, and hopes to staff up within the next year with four classes of 50.
chapters.title: Salaam asks about current DOP vacancies and hiring timeline

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm going to yield my questions for Councilmember Salam to ask of you.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.text: Just a few questions regarding DOP oversight and the staffing in the workforce.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: I'm not sure if this was answered already because I kind of came in and they were talking about some of the staffing issues.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: But as of March of 2026, DOP reported a 23% vacancy rate with

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: 255 vacancies, including 210 probation officers since fiscal year 2023.

utterances.text: DOP lost 405.

utterances.text: What is the vacancy count today and what is the hiring target and timelines to close the probation officer gap?

chapters.title: Salaam asks about juvenile rearrest increase; Dessimore cites staffing and unit alignment

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Is it morning still?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We have overall 171 vacancy rates.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And of that, 134 are probation officer in the probation officer series.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We plan on hopefully...

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Staffing up within the next year with the four classes coming in at 50.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So we should be in good shape by then.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And in terms of outcomes and performances, juvenile rearrest rates rose 50% over, rose 50%.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Over that, over what period from what base number and to what does DOP attribute the increase to?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Can you repeat the last part of your question?

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: So the juvenile rearrest rate rose 50%.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Over what period, from what base number, and to what does DOP attribute the increase?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Well, I think part of it, as we know, and we talked about just staffing is one issue, and we are improving with that.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Also, just in terms of the alignment of the units, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Officers were carrying sometimes six and seven different units, whether low, high, and moderate.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: So we, with all the boroughs, we are making changes to that so that the officers are

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: identified as high-risk officers, those that are moderate and those that are low, to make sure that it's right-sizing and one-size for those young people.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And I think that it's easier to manage for the officers and then making sure we also lower the caseloads for those higher-risk population.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Another thing is that it's very important that we...

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Meet with those young people immediately, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We find out what is going on.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We sit with that young person to set goals and to see what they need and also just to figure out what is driving the behavior, right?

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: And it's always about...

utterances.text: And also with our community-based organizations, we are pulling them in to help us with that process.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore

utterances.text: And since this commission has been here, we are making improvements within the last six months.

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: Even though it's small percentage, we are...

utterances.speaker: Stacey Dessimore
utterances.text: We are hopeful that we are moving in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: I know, like, jobs and, you know, meaningful employment definitely goes a long way, especially for young people, because, you know, if you're doing things that might not necessarily be productive in society, then you fall back into old things.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: You know, I'll never forget my good friend Les Brown said, if you can't see it,

utterances.text: You can't be it.

utterances.speaker: Yusef Salaam
utterances.text: And so a lot of times it's those examples that you can see in front of you that really will help you to change for the better.

utterances.text: How are the programs aligned?

utterances.text: You are doing what you can, but I don't know if you can make sure that every kind of program that's needed is available.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, I know, for instance, I have a friend whose daughter is mentally ill.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: She got arrested, tried to kill her mother and her brother.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And, you know, it's hard.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There aren't a lot of programs to fit her.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We spent two days, the two of us, calling around.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We found one that might work, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how do we need other kinds of programs?

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what kinds of programs DOP needs or whether existing programs need more capacity. Goodwin says DOP is reassessing and identifies employment, mental health and behavioral health, and housing as main components, and is mapping available resources.
chapters.title: Brewer asks what programs are needed; Goodwin cites employment, mental health, housing

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are you finding that there are sufficient alternatives?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because these young people need a lot of support.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We are looking at the programs that we are utilizing now, and in fact, I'm convening a meeting

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: in the coming weeks with other community-based organizations to talk about programming

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: and talking about availability and what they have, and is there any way that probation may be helpful in terms of extending or providing them with resources.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: They can take more people.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So right now, within the two weeks, under Andy, Annie Minguez, we're going to work together to look at that at probation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So what kind of programs do you think you need, or is it just more capacity in the programs that are there?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You have some very, you know, even when you're doing intensive, like you talked about with some of the young people, they may not have a place to live.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: etc.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's not like even a program can help.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether public schools help with programs for students and raises housing needs. Eusebio says DOP had classrooms in NEON sites and is rebuilding that relationship, and says DOP works with DHS on housing as a stabilizing factor.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about DOE and housing; Eusebio cites NEON classrooms and DHS partnership

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We almost need housing, in my opinion, for some young people.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I wish we could be looking at that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just want to hear from you what you need.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: One of the things I think, that's what I need is to make sure we reassess what we have first.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I got nine months under my belt, so I'm looking at employment.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We're looking at mental health, behavioral health.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: We're looking at housing.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: These are the main components that we need at probation.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So we are definitely looking at it.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Like I said, I've been convening with different organizations to look at capacity, which is very important.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: I need to know what capacity is.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Are there programs we are missing?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: There's a lot of resources in New York City, and some of them go overlooked.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So I need to know what that is.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So we're mapping at this point.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks DOP to let the chair know what it needs after reassessing programs so the council can address gaps in budget season. Eusebio says DOP will come back for support and stresses collective work through the NEON model.
chapters.title: Brewer asks DOP to report assessment needs for budget; Eusebio agrees to collaborate

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And the Department of Education, or whatever the hell it's called, New York City Public Schools, I hate that name.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because it's a noun.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It makes no sense to me.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But anyway, do they help in some way with some of the programs that are for older students?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Or even younger students?

utterances.text: So from our history working with probation, we had a close relation with DOE.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: And we're going back to the roots.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Because we actually had classrooms in some of our NEON sites.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: That's a way how we supported not just people on probation, but also community members at large across the city.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So we are very much looking at assessing, as Commissioner indicated, but also looking at other things that are innovative, from AI to things that are more attractive to the people that we serve.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And what about housing?

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers pivots to the intelligence unit and asks how many probation officers are assigned there. McKenzie says the unit has 14 probation officers, 10 supervising probation officers, two branch chiefs, and one associate commissioner.
chapters.title: Chair asks how many officers are in the intelligence unit; McKenzie lists staffing

utterances.text: There was nothing left.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And if it wasn't for her grandmother, who happens to be a friend of mine, she'd be on the street.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So housing, obviously, is a stabilizing factor in the life of everyone, not just young people.

utterances.text: And it's something that we work continuously.

utterances.text: In fact, we also work in establishing a relationship with DHS, who is one of our partners, you know, through the NEON.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So we look into seeing, and by the way, we're not just stopping there.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: It's also seeing what other out-of-the-box thinking we can do to support people in that space as well.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Can you let the chair?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: know when you have your assessment what it is that you need because I hope that during the budget season we're not going to bring I don't think you're going to bring those numbers down if you don't have the programs that you are

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether someone can apply directly into the intelligence unit rather than coming up through the ranks. McKenzie says someone with a specific skill set like cyber might be pulled in, but DOP generally prefers officers with adult or juvenile field experience.
chapters.title: Chair asks if officers can apply directly to intelligence; McKenzie prefers field experience

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: reassessing I can't believe it's not going to be easy there's lots of gaps so you'll let us know where you are in terms of

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Reassessing?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Obviously, we will come back and get your support as well because we believe that everyone has a stake here as a city.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: To do better, we all got to work collectively, and that's part of our NEOM model, right?

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether intelligence unit members supervise clients. McKenzie says they do not directly supervise clients and instead support case probation officers.
chapters.title: Chair asks if intelligence unit carries caseloads; McKenzie says no direct supervision

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Everyone plays a role here.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers cites a 2025 report that 44% of NEON Works participants learned about the program from friends or family while only 18% learned from DOP. Goodwin says that was past practice and DOP hired a strategic initiatives and engagement officer to change direction.
chapters.title: Chair asks about NEON Works awareness; Goodwin says past practice will change

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I just wanted to add that we will be making our rounds with city council.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sounds great.

utterances.text: Next, I want to pivot to intelligence unit.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How many probation officers are in the intelligence unit?

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: So we have 14 probation officers, 10 supervising probation officers, two branch chiefs, and one associate commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What are the intelligence unit's primary responsibilities and how does it coordinate with the NYPD and other law enforcement agencies?

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: There are different units in particular, for example, would be our cyber, our cyber unit.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: We also have an officer that's detailed to Haida.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: And another with the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Marshals Task Force.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Previously, Intel was decentralized, and it's now been re-centralized.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Like every other part of the agency, we also need more officers in the intelligence division as well.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: So we're very slowly and deliberately rebuilding.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And someone could apply directly into that position versus coming up the ranks?

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers cites a 2025 report on barriers like school, jobs, caregiving, safety, and mental health support. Eusebio says NEON taps community resources and DOP is redoubling stakeholder engagement to connect clients to services, and Goodwin says the work is in process.
chapters.title: Chair asks about barriers to NEON participation; Eusebio says DOP is addressing them

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: So if, for example, we come across someone who's got a specific skill set, right, let's say in the cyber area, yeah, that person might be pulled.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: But generally speaking, we like individuals who've had experience in the field, whether it be adult.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Or juvenile operations so they can better support those operations.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Do any members of the intelligence unit have a caseload where they must supervise clients?

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: They don't directly supervise clients.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: They should be working with the case PO in that regard.

utterances.speaker: Wayne McKenzie
utterances.text: Intel is more of a support than a caseload bearing division.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: A report commissioned by the Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity from June 2025 noted that a large plurality, roughly 44%, of people who learned about the Neon Works program, bless you,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Learned about it from friends or family while only 18% of people learned about it from the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is that a trend with other NEON programs as well?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And does this indicate that most participants are not necessarily Department of Probation clients?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: It was a past practice, but it won't be moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And that's why we hired our DCF strategic initiatives and engagement.

chapters.title: Chair asks if program staffing is vendor responsibility; Goodwin says collaborative

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: And so we are definitely moving in a different direction.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But with the past policy, was that indicative that most participants were not necessarily clients of Department of Probation?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin

utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers thanks the DOP panel for its testimony and responses. She dismisses the panel.
chapters.title: Chair dismisses DOP panel after testimony

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: But we're looking to make sure that it's 60% client, 40% community.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Why that number?

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Because we want to make sure that all of our clients is getting the services and the resources needed to help us engage in making sure that they're serviced first.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers opens the hearing to public testimony and reminds attendees that decorum must be observed. She explains that speakers get two minutes, written testimony can be submitted, and audio or video recordings are not accepted as testimony.
chapters.title: Chair opens public testimony and gives decorum instructions

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: But we're still open to having community involved.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So the NEON, by definition, is about tapping into all the resources that we can bear at a given community.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: And by and large, whether it's behavioral health services or vocational mentoring opportunities, they open to everyone in that community.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: And significantly, our job now is to make sure that our clients are also connected to the services at hand.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But has the department addressed any of those issues?

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: So let me go up front and say that's what we're doing right now.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: We sort of redoubling, working with a stakeholder.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Again, that was something that the commission underscored in her testimony.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: Engaging the stakeholder, by definition, is about that.

utterances.speaker: Robert Eusebio
utterances.text: It's about making sure that what matters to that community is happening, whether it's a type of programming that is needed, if there's a gap, that we can be there up front and able to engage them.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: So in short, are we addressing it?

chapters.title: Chair calls first public panel: Powell, Peoples, and Lee

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: It's in process.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Goodwin
utterances.text: At this time.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Given that the department is weathering a general staff recruitment and retention, I don't want to call it a crisis anymore because it seems like you guys are doing significant work around that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers

chapters.summary: Youngmi Lee of Brooklyn Defender Services says DOP can influence sentencing through pre-sentence investigation reports and often recommends jail or prison despite promised probation. She asks DOP to allow attorneys to attend probation interviews without a court order and to stop encouraging clients to deny guilt.
chapters.title: Youngmi Lee testifies on PSI recommendations and access to counsel during probation interviews

utterances.text: I think it's a collaborative approach.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: I appreciate the testimony and the responses today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
