chapters.summary: Lee asks DOP to recommend certificates of relief from civil disabilities in every probation report to help people obtain employment and licenses. She also urges DOP to restore early termination for people who have completed probation conditions, noting that clean slate relief depends on early termination.
chapters.title: Youngmi Lee urges CRD recommendations and early termination of probation

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: I'm an attorney at Brooklyn Defender Services, a public defender office where we represent thousands of individuals in both Brooklyn and in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: First of all, I just want to say that BDS is and remains optimistic that the Department of Probation will go back to being

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: an agency that supports rehabilitation versus being a very much law enforcement, us against you type of agency.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: I want to talk about the power of the Department of Probation, specifically about three areas, although there are more.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: And I know I only have one minute left.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: I do want to talk about certificates of relief from civil disabilities, access to counsel during

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: pre-sentence investigation report interviews with the Department of Probation, as well as the early termination program.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: First, probation has a huge role in determining whether someone could receive a prison sentence, a jail sentence, or a non-incarceratory sentence,

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: even after an agreed-upon plea.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: And I say this because oftentimes when a person pleads guilty and the promised sentence is probation,

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: The court will order what's called an INS report, a PSR.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: They're all the same, a pre-sentence investigation report.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: That report is done by a probation officer who, at the end, can make a recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: Oftentimes we find, especially in the last few years, the recommendation has always been jail or prison despite the promised sentence of probation.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: We also find that probation officers can and will encourage people to deny their guilt, which then results in the court saying the promised sentence of probation is off the table,

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: and sometimes judges will threaten hearings, and obviously the person can depart from the promised sentence and send someone to prison.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: My one minute is up.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I am going to let you continue because we are light on public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So for this panel, because you are the defenders and the union, we will accommodate.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: I'll try to be a lot quicker.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: We learned after the Harvey Weinstein trial in 2020 that attorneys can attend these probation interviews, but only upon a court order.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: I have been told by judges that they will grant these requests.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: I would just ask probation to streamline the process and that whenever an attorney can and wants to attend these probation interviews, that the attorney just be allowed to without a court order.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: It should be just the default.

chapters.summary: Natalie Peoples of the Legal Aid Society says Intro 1104 does not go far enough because intake interviews happen post-arrest and pre-filing before counsel is assigned. She says decisions made during that interview can affect the long-term posture of a child's case and asks that counsel be required at that stage.
chapters.title: Natalie Peoples testifies on Intro 1104 and need for counsel at intake

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: I also want to talk about certificates of relief from civil disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: Again, this has a lot to do with rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: BDS has worked with the Department of Probation actually doing CRD drives within the community at different locations.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: While a CRD is not the end all in terms of people being able to obtain employment, it certainly helps, especially when there are legal barriers to employment, such as security guard licenses

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: or TLC licenses.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: By getting a certificate of relief from civil disabilities, many people can

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: obtain such employment.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: In the old days, the Department of Probation had a policy where all probation reports also had a recommendation about CRDs.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: We have seen that practice fall out of place, and we are asking probation to again

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: recommend CRDs whenever a probation report is completed, especially obviously when a person is going to receive a sentence of probation.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: When someone gets a prison sentence, probation doesn't have any control over that and the person has to be recommended for a CRD by the parole board.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: So I would just ask that probation, again, bring back that practice where every PSI has a recommendation attached.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: Finally, early termination of probation.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: There was some testimony earlier about the early termination program, but I do want to emphasize that there are many people who are serving.

chapters.summary: Peoples says DOP promised in March to end punitive practices and provide more support, but she has not seen those changes 10 months into the administration. She asks DOP to keep communication open with defense counsel, expand alternatives to incarceration, and change court practices.
chapters.title: Natalie Peoples says DOP remains punitive and asks for culture change

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: Up to five years of probation on a felony sentence, and oftentimes that is unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: Within five years, a person has usually completed all of their conditions of probation.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: They need to be terminated from probation early, successfully.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: And I say this because in order for a clean slate,

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: to actually take effect, the person has to be terminated from probation or parole so that they can get an earlier

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: ceiling of their convictions.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: The same is true for misdemeanors.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: A sentence of probation on a misdemeanor can last up to three years, which is at times inordinately long when a person has already satisfied all the conditions of probation.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: And with that, I will complete my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: My name is Natalie Peoples.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: I'm the attorney in charge of youth justice policy and training at the juvenile rights practice of the Legal Aid Society.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: Our juvenile practice combined with our criminal practice represents most of the children that are charged with crimes in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: And we intend to submit written remarks in addition to what I say today.

chapters.summary: Dalvney Powell, president of the United Probation Officers Association, says probation officers are underpaid relative to their peace officer responsibilities. She cites EEOC and federal lawsuits and analyses showing men earn nearly $5,000 more than women and white men earn about $14,500 more than women of color in DOP.
chapters.title: Dalvney Powell testifies on underpayment and pay disparities in probation

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: I want to thank you for holding this hearing to discuss the current policies and culture of the Department of Probation as well as 1104.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: I want to first take maybe 30 seconds to discuss 1104.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: While we applaud the intent of the bill, what we're talking about here is a time that is post-arrest,

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: pre-filing, pre-assignment of counsel, and the decisions that are made during that process, during that interview process by the child and their responsible adult

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: can affect the long-term posture of their case, which affects the long-term posture of a child's life.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: We think that this bill does not go far enough and that counsel should be required at that stage for

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: those for that interview and for the important decisions that are made during that time period.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: The language both in the bill and also in the Family Court Act about what information can be disclosed at what stage in the proceeding is confusing and it's complicated and we find a lot of our clients don't necessarily understand it which is why it's

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: immensely important for counsel to be involved that early in the process.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: Now, in March of this year, the Department of Probation made some promises.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: They promised that they would no longer continue punitive practices and tactics of the previous administration, that they would be more and provide more support.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: Towards our clients, towards our client population.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: We were hopeful that, you know, 10 months into this administration that we would see those changes, and we haven't yet seen those changes.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: We are still seeing a punitive carceral stance from the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: Can I just take a couple more seconds?

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: So while I do thank them for their testimony during this hearing, there are a couple things that I am asking for the Department of Probation to do.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: First of all is to keep the pathways of communication open with defense counsel.

chapters.summary: Powell says inadequate compensation is driving experienced officers to NYPD, Correction, and neighboring probation departments, increasing caseloads and reducing time for home visits and case planning. She urges the City Council to extend collective bargaining protections to probation officers and says safe decarceration requires strong, fairly compensated probation.
chapters.title: Powell links low pay to staffing crisis and urges collective bargaining protections

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: That is essential.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: We are here to partner with them, especially for our clients, to help our clients succeed.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: We're asking for them to expand alternatives to incarceration programs, both for family court as well as the youth part, for creating programs with science-backed methodologies.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: We're also asking for a change in their culture and for that change in culture to filter down to the practices that are happening in court every day.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: Use the mic, please.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Good morning, Honorable Chair Brooks Powers and distinguished members of the City Council Criminal Justice Committee.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: My name is Dalvney Powell, President of the United Probation Office Association.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I have with me Vice President Gail Seeley, who's also a court liaison supervisor in the Bronx for adult services.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Secretary of the Union James Green is also a CLO for family court and family court services, and he also works the evening intake on the weekends.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Weekend arraignment.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: For decades, New York City probation officers have been underpaid relative to their responsibilities as peace officers.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: We supervise justice-involved individuals throughout the five boroughs by conducting home and community visits, enforcing court orders, responding to violations and crises, preparing reports to help judges make critical decisions.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: This work has specific goals helping to reduce recidivism and help our clients lead more productive lives.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Despite the role that we play in reducing incarceration, our compensation has failed to reflect the risk and demands of our public safety work.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: This inequity is a racial and gender justice issue.

chapters.summary: Powell says probation officers now have 11 steps but top pay is about $81,000 after 11 years, while parole officers start at $81,000 and neighboring counties pay over $100,000. She says the city trains officers who then leave for better pay, and calls for proper compensation to retain staff.
chapters.title: Powell details salary comparisons and retention concerns

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: As the workforce became increasingly composed of women and people of color, our members'compensation failed to keep pace with the growing responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: UPOA filed an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission complaint alleging discrimination in compensation.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: In 2021, UPOA and five women of color filed a federal lawsuit challenging disparities in pay and promotional opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Data cited in that litigation shows significant disparities.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: In New York City, public advocate analysis found that men in the Department of Probation earn nearly $5,000 more on average than women.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: An analysis commissioned by UPOA found that white men earn approximately $14,500 more on average than women of color within the Department of Probation.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Today, inadequate compensation is contributing to the staffing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Experienced probation officers are leaving for better paying law enforcement positions in New York City to the New York City Police Department, Department of Correction, and neighboring probation departments, among other employers where their skills and experience

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: are compensated more competitively.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: As a result, employees of the Department of Probation have experienced increased case loads and longer hours.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Officers have less time for home visits, individualized case planning, treatment coordination, and other intensive work that effective community supervision requires.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: According to data we obtained from the department,

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: There are approximately 594 probation professionals, of which 41.4% are under five years at the department, and 21.7% have 20 years or more.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: to August 2026, there were approximately 449 separations.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I'm still trying to figure out what the real numbers are, and that was including over 300 resignations.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Also, from 2020 to the present, it appears to have been appears to staffing has declined by 33.2%.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: When probation officers leave,

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Public safety suffers.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: As New York City increasingly relies on alternatives to incarceration, it cannot afford to lose professionals responsible for effective community supervision.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: We urge City Council to amend administrative code to extend appropriate collective bargaining protections to probation officers at its

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: that it previously did for emergency medical personnel.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: You cannot have safe decarceration without strong probation, and you cannot have strong probation without fairly compensated workers.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and attention to this critical issue.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I'm happy to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Can I just add something while I'm on the mic?

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I'm on the mic, right?

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: One, two.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: You talked about doing analysis.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I think I have given you some data from before, and I've been doing analysis in comparison to...

utterances.speaker: Youngmi Lee
utterances.text: I appreciate this.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: That's the staffing and the separation.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: But before I gave you something on the dollars and cents, because in order to know how to fix the problem, right?

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: So I'm going to give you something more updated, because recently the data I gave you before has changed because parole, sheriff's office, and...

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: And Suffolk County has new contracts.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: So to me, it's so bad that our, let me just go back.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: My last contract negotiations, I was able to get us to from zero steps to 11 steps to try to make the job more attractive, right?

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: We are now, so we got 11 steps now, which we didn't have.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers thanks Powell and says she wants conversations before the budget cycle about making probation jobs more attractive. She notes DOP will be important as the city transitions from Rikers Island to borough-based jails and calls for a holistic funding conversation.
chapters.title: Chair responds to Powell on budget talks and Rikers transition

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: And now our top salaries for probation officers, $81,000, where that's the 11 years, whereas the parole officers walking into the door at $81,000.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: These are the things that we're dealing with, right?

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: We might have 11 steps.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Whereas Suffolk County, Nassau County, and on the other side counties, they might have 11 or 12 steps, but what they get at the end of those 11 or 12 steps is over 100,000.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: So the thing, my concern, our concern is that somebody, the city, is wasting taxpayers'money.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: And throwing it away because probation is doing an excellent job in training them, but then they go on and take those skill sets and they move on to other places.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: So, right.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: So you asked the question of what the problem is.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether public defenders' clients are prepared for intake interviews and whether counsel should be present. Peoples says many youth go through intake pre-filing before the right to counsel attaches, so defenders are often not involved, and says the Family Court Act allows intake information to be used post-fact-finding.
chapters.title: Chair asks public defenders about Intro 1104 and intake preparedness; Peoples explains right to counsel

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Commissioner Goodwin is doing a wonderful job.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: We came in together.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I've been here for 40 years.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I've done family court, adult court.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I'm a supervisor by civil service title.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I know probation.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I live it.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I sleep it.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I know both sides of the table.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: We're working together with the department to try to build up the agency.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: But it's like grains of sand.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: You can put that grains of sand in your hand, and all it's going to do is seep through.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: If we don't face reality that probation officers need to be paid properly, what are we doing?

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I'm coming back, and I'm going to keep saying the same thing over and over again.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: But this is real.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: For y'all to work, we have to have the proper staffing, absolutely, but we have to have the compensation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I offer the same to you as I did to the commissioner in terms of wanting to have conversations ahead of the upcoming budget cycle so that we can understand what are we advocating for that can

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: make it more attractive to talent to come into these positions to do this job.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because as we are looking to transition from Rikers Island to borough-based jails,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: the Department of Probation is going to be an important element to this, as well as the public defenders and the work that you all do, too.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks what information young people and families would most benefit from knowing before an intake interview. Peoples says families should know what kinds of cases probation will not accept for adjustment so they do not subject themselves to unnecessary inquiry.
chapters.title: Chair asks what families need before intake; Peoples says which cases won't be adjusted

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Like, we need to have a holistic conversation on what that looks like, what the dollar tag truly is, and how we are able to meet that need.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I want to also acknowledge we've been joined by Council Member Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I did have a couple of questions, and then I'll yield to my colleagues for questions as well.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: First, with the public defenders regarding the bill that I'm introducing today, Intro 1104, in your experience, do your clients seem prepared for intake interviews?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I can only imagine how overwhelming that may feel from a parent's perspective, going into a room, not knowing what's going on with your kid or even a young person going in and being.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks Powell how workload feels different since January. Powell says the office environment is better but members are still suffering from the previous administration, officers are still leaving, and the union recently lost a whole gun unit in Queens.
chapters.title: Chair asks Powell about workload and retention; Powell says better but officers still leaving

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: read, you know, their

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: rights, if you will, in terms of what the next steps and stages may be for them.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So I just wanted to understand through your lens, do you feel that, and I think you kind of spoke to it saying that we should be adding that the lawyers should be present.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I thought that was a very helpful point, but if you had to, if you wanted to elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: I think what's confusing about

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: about the intake interview is for every kid that family court has original jurisdiction over, those kids go through that intake process

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: pre-filing, which means for public defenders, the right to counsel has not yet attached.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: So unless for them it's a prior client of ours or, you know,

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: you know, we represent them on a child protective case, we aren't necessarily involved.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: So we don't know about it necessarily.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How does that impact like their protection?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So for example, when someone's arrested, it's like, you know, you get Reg and Miranda rights and you know what's being held against you if you say something crazy.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But in that instance, because the lawyer has not been assigned yet,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is that young person now vulnerable to anything that can be held against them in the path that they get to navigate in the Department of Probation?

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: In the way the Family Court Act is written, the information that's obtained during that intake interview cannot be used pre-fact finding, but it can be used post-fact finding.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: And so they're incorporated into the reports.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: The other population that we're talking about are cases that are removed from the youth part.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether the reasons officers leave differ from before the current mayoral administration. Powell says the problem is historical and inherited, and that the last contract had to revamp salary steps and give up vacation days to raise starting pay.
chapters.title: Chair asks if reasons for leaving changed; Powell says salary issues are historical

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: For those kids, council has already attached because it attached in the youth part.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: And then we continue, I think both of our organizations continue that representation.

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: So we take part in that intake interview, which is why we know so much about what happens, the questions that are asked, what that looks like.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And what information do you think young people and their families would most benefit from knowing prior to an intake interview?

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: First, what kind of cases are that probation will not accept them for adjustment?

utterances.speaker: Natalie Peoples
utterances.text: Because then I'm not saying that there's no point in having the interview, but there's no point subjecting yourself to that kind of inquiry that early in the stage of your case if you know that there's no way that your case is ever going to be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That was very helpful.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Davine, I wanted to ask you a question regarding workload and retention.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Since January, how does your workload feel different?

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: The environment is better at the office, I mean, at probation, but the members are still suffering because we're still recuperating from the previous administration.

chapters.summary: Council Member Brewer asks whether there are enough alternatives and programs outside probation to meet the needs of people they serve. She says her experience is that programs are insufficient and notes the commissioner is reassessing.
chapters.title: Brewer asks public defenders and union about availability of alternatives

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I mean, I want to go forward, but it's better, but we still have that residue, and they're still leaving.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: They're still leaving.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I just wanted to tell you this, too.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: My last contract, we increased the starting salary by 33% to $61,000.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: So we have the highest starting salary.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Which is good, but the issue is retaining them.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Before Commissioner Goodman came on, we lost a whole unit in Queens of the gun unit, a whole unit.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: And we're about to lose a significant amount of probation officers in a couple of weeks when parole starts to hire.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: They're ready to go.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: So it's better.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: But it keeps going.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: I don't want to keep repeating it, but it goes back to the salaries.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I was going to just ask, like, if the reasons given by offices for leaving different from before the start of the current mayoral administration or if it's in the same.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: It's historical.

chapters.summary: Powell says there was significant programming before the previous administration and DOP is now rebuilding. Peoples says good programs fill up and have waiting lists, and Lee says funding cuts eliminated vital programs and more ATD and ATI programs are needed to reduce juvenile detention.
chapters.title: Powell, Peoples, and Lee respond on program capacity and funding cuts

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: This was inherited.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: So, you know, when I became the president, I did an analysis of our salaries.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: And I realized we was never going to meet, get to where we need to be to be in comparison to our competition, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: And we had to practically, this last contract, revamp, give up two days of vacation in order to try to get the 11 years and get the starting salary to where we are now.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: So this is historical, but I think it's time to fix it.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: Because we can do better services for your clients and other clients in the community at large.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: And everybody wins.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: So in all due respect, it's great that we're having this oversight hearing for probation.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: And I don't know how much input the department and I would love to be a part of that conversation with you.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: But I think we should also, this is just a suggestion, all due respect, have OLR, have OMB, have those oversight agencies at the table and DCAS.

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: What's the issue?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And there's more to come.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you for all that you're doing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I guess my question is similar.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have in your work see that there are enough alternatives for young people or anybody actually for the programs that they need?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because it's always been my experience that there aren't enough and the commissioner kind of hinted that she's reassessing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All of you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah, whatever.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The question is, are there enough programs outside of probation that have the needs met, that meet the needs of the people you're serving?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Sort of alternatives or programs that they need that are obvious for their...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: To be successful?

utterances.speaker: Dalvney Powell
utterances.text: There was a point prior to the administration, there was a significant amount of programming.

chapters.summary: Powell points to evening intake and weekend arraignment programs as another way DOP tries to keep youth out of detention. She says James Green works in those programs.
chapters.title: Powell notes evening intake and weekend arraignment programs

summary: The Committee on Criminal Justice held an oversight hearing on the Department of Probation's organizational strategy and Intro 1104, which would provide youth accused of crimes with information about the criminal legal process.

Commissioner Sharon Goodwin testified on staffing and recruitment, risk-based caseload right-sizing, rebuilding court and community relationships, and DOP's support for Intro 1104; council members questioned vacancies, juvenile rearrests, early termination, court liaisons, intelligence staffing, and community programs.

Public defenders, the probation officers union, youth advocates, and community members testified on pay disparities, access to counsel during intake, program restoration, mentorship, and alternatives to incarceration.
